title: BlackRock dials down risk amid Middle East disruption - Investor Daily

Long a confident backer of US stocks and the AI trade, the world’s largest asset manager has made a notable move to reduce risk this week. In the firm’s latest Weekly Market Commentary, BlackRock global chief investment strategist Wei Li outlined what the firm is calling a backdrop of “durable disruption” caused by the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran, and explained the tactical investment changes the team is making in response. “The energy forward market is now pricing in a durable disruption, reflecting the attack on energy infrastructure in the region that will take time to recover from and a possible prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “This ushers in a supercharged version of a world shaped by supply. And unless there is tangible evidence of action that could shorten the duration of this broad supply disruption, in our view there is little basis to think that the market expectations for elevated energy prices next year are too high,” Li said. She said these levels represent an inflation, growth and rate shock that is “not consistent with overall risk asset pricing”, adding that central banks are finding themselves in increasingly difficult territory. It comes as Brent crude rose 1.8 per cent to US$104.04 on 26 March. In turn, BlackRock has brought down US broad equities from modest overweight to neutral. It has also downgraded Japanese equities from modest overweight to neutral, citing its outsized reliance on energy as a concern. North Asian economies are viewed as particularly vulnerable to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz given their reliance on energy imports. The changes mean the firm is now neutral across all equities. For bonds, Li said BlackRock continues to favour the front end and belly of the curve over long-dated Treasuries. The stance echoes recent comments from Pitcher Partners , which noted that global investors remain wary of longer-dated bonds despite Australian bond yields climbing to decade highs this week. BlackRock is also bringing up short duration European government bonds from neutral to modest overweight to “add a bit of cash buffer”, noting market repricing for European Central Bank (ECB) hikes. Insight Investment recently made the case for European credit amid the current geopolitical backdrop. Looking ahead, BlackRock said it stands ready to adjust risk exposure as the picture clears, leaving the door open to de-escalation. However, it cautioned the situation “may well be more painful than it looked initially in the early days of the conflict.” Broader retreat from US shares BlackRock’s US equity downgrade comes amid a broader retreat from US equities, with Australian ETF investors increasingly favouring domestic equity funds over global, US-heavy picks. Speaking to Investor Daily, Sharesies’ head of capital markets, Jacki Neumann said she has observed retail investors becoming more cautious toward the major US tech names that have long dominated the index. “We’ve seen net selling across several ‘Magnificent Seven’ names on the Sharesies platform since early March,” Neumann said. Fortunes have recently shifted for the mega-cap tech names that dominated the S&P 500 for years, with Meta down 20 per cent over the six months to 26 March. It comes as questions mount over excessive AI capital expenditure and private market debt financing by such companies. At the same time, Neumann stressed the rotation isn’t panic selling, arguing investors are simply gravitating toward companies with strong fundamentals, resilient balance sheets and durable competitive moats. It echoes a broader argument that the tech sell-off is separating the more defensible AI plays from those more exposed as the sector enters a new era. BlackRock was also keen to note that for all the turbulence, the S&P 500 sits only 7 per cent below its February record peak. Nevertheless, BlackRock’s de-risking activity adds to a broader bearish turn, with the latest Bank of America (BofA) survey showing investors made their largest allocations to cash in six years this month.
